comments.author: kristopolous
comments.text:
I've been working on something in a similar class for about a year called llcat
It came out of a lack of their being an LLM-native tool that feels like cURL or other unix-friendly things such as awk or sed.
I wanted something stateless, explicit, low-level, and composable without "settings" just like you don't with grep or sort.
Instead, you can index into files with jq or line numbers and save invocations for later for instance
llcat --save invocation.json \
-k "@~/credentials.txt:12" \
-u "@settings.json:.[3].host" \
-s "@system_prompts:8" \
-m "@settings.json:.[3].model" \
"@query.txt:12" > output.txt
and then
llcat --load invocation.json { ... parameters you want to override ... }
Conversations are stored as JSON files and you can have a different one input and output. This means you can do stuff like
for i in *; do
cat "$i" | llcat --load settings.json -cr context.json  > ../results/"${i}.output"
done
And use a non-mutable conversation to apply the same context over a group of files.
Since there's no hidden state you can use it in shell scripts and get operational guarantees.
For instance, I have this line in a separate project
sc_pane="${pane_list[0]}" llcat "$dry" \
-c "$con

The one part that sort of surprises me is he says "The second thing we are missing is that the Model has not in fact found a way of obtaining
a program with g < m. (Moreover, Fable tells me this is impossible, but I do not follow the argument yet.)"
I'm not sure what argument fable gave him, but this part seems not horribly difficult to prove.  I'm sure i'm missing something since i'm not that great at this kind of math.
The short reason is that each slice call can at most double the number of nonzero entries, but a transform that would enable g < m must turn a single nonzero entry into (2^m) nonzero entries in a single call.
Since the permutes can't generate non-zero entries (since they only move things around), you actually need
exactly
m slice calls in the initial 2-instruction model given (where you can only do slices and permutes) precisely
because
of the need to create 2^m non-zero entries where each individual slice op can only double the number (and permutes do nothing)

https://gist.github.com/dberlin/e785c51aff0285c9c0a3ea0f24fa...

This looks like it's using the emSign root path, which is useful, but the AAA root path is equally useful in different cases. The AAA root path was disabled for https on root stores newer than February 2025, but has been in root stores since forever. Meanwhile the emSign root path was only included in root stores since ~2018 and got removed in October 2026.
So from the perspective of hacking old IoT devices, if your device hasn't been updated since 2018, the AAA path should work; if since February 2025, either path works; if since October 2026, the emSign path.

Looks cool!
One aspect of multi-user agent security, which I think is underexplored, is how context from a higher-privileged session might "leak" into a lower privileged session.
